title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Opened Fire on Students
dek: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.
why: This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the event, and it directly helps in understanding the social fractures in America in the 1960s and 70s.
who: Viewers interested in American social movements of the 1960s and 70s, militarized policing, or historical conflict, especially those concerned with abuse of power and civil rights.

points.h: The National Guard enters campus under arms
points.body: On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen carrying M1 rifles, bayonets and tear gas entered Kent State University, bivouacking at the football field and guarding the ROTC building. This deployment enraged students; even those who had not been involved in the protests felt the war had come to their doorstep. But the students were not especially afraid, because the Guard had previously handled demonstrations with tear gas or brawls, and had never shot anyone. What was unusual this time was that the troops carried live ammunition.

points.h: Orders are confused, and the governor pours fuel on the fire
points.body: Governor Rhodes's speech was full of inflammatory rhetoric, comparing the protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the KKK and calling them "the worst people in America." But in fact his order formally deploying the Guard did not come until May 5, while the troops had already arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government and the governor over the Guard's mission: the president believed assemblies had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban had not yet taken effect. This confused transmission of information laid the groundwork for the later clash.

points.h: Rules changed midstream, triggering a standoff
points.body: On the evening of May 3, students gathered in the plaza to protest, but local government moved the curfew up from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as "changing the rules midway," and split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down on the main road, blocking traffic and singing "Give Peace a Chance." Police and the Guard surrounded them, with helicopters circling overhead. In the end the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to drive the students back to their dormitories, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

points.h: May 4: a peaceful assembly forms again
points.body: At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered in the plaza again. Although no official state of emergency existed, university officials handed out leaflets saying the assembly was illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the gathering through loudspeakers. By noon the assembly was largely peaceful, with only some crude slogans. University police announced through loudspeakers that the assembly was illegal and demanded dispersal, but their voices were drowned out, and a few rocks flew at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two rounds of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away.

The Guard advanced to clear the area and succeeded in dispersing most of the protesters, but one group of 52 pushed too far and was trapped in the fenced stadium, pelted with rocks. Ten minutes later they received orders to withdraw and moved toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned, raised their weapons and fired a 13-second volley, 67 bullets in all. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away) and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Nine others were wounded, the nearest 60 feet away and the farthest 750 feet away.

After the shooting there was dead silence, and students stood frozen in place. Fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt beside Jeffrey Miller's body screaming, and 21-year-old photography student John Filo took the picture, which became an image that shook the nation. But the conflict did not end; protests spread across the country, followed by the Hard Hat Riot, the Jackson State shootings and other events. The episode stresses that this history is strikingly similar to the present and worth reflecting on.
